title: 2026-11-04 GPU runtime profiling - TensorRT/vLLM/CUDA graphs deep dive with Helix Robotics
summary: Deep dive into GPU runtime profiling to address Helix Robotics' latency spikes and cost concerns. Compared TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM execution characteristics, discussed kernel selection heuristics, CUDA graph warmup behavior, KV cache sizing, batching tradeoffs, and on-prem/VPC constraints. Agreed to run a 48-hour benchmark using Helix's RL inference workload and share kernel-level traces and TensorRT engine configs.
topics: KV cache sizing and eviction policies
Quantization impacts (int8/4-bit) on throughput and accuracy
VPC/on-prem deployment considerations and GPU isolation
action_items: Samir Patel: Share TensorRT engine config, cudagraph traces, and vLLM profiling scripts by 2026-11-09
Priya Rao: Provide representative RL inference prompts and a 24h load script by 2026-11-06
Aisha Chen: Set up a shared S3 bucket and grant access to Helix logs by 2026-11-05
Daniel Kim: Share on-prem GPU cluster topology (nodes, GPU types, driver/cuda versions) by 2026-11-06
next_steps: Run 48h benchmark on Helix payload with TensorRT-LLM and vLLM configs (Redwood + Helix)
Exchange kernel-level traces and look at cudagraph warmup profiles
Schedule follow-up 30m call to review benchmark results week of 2026-11-16
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-11-04
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~65 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Aisha Chen (Redwood SE), Marco Diaz (Redwood Perf), Michael Torres (Helix CTO), Priya Rao (Helix ML), Daniel Kim (Helix Platform), Sara Liu (Helix SRE)

Summary (auto): Deep technical profiling session focusing on GPU runtime choices, kernel selection, and cudagraph interactions affecting latency and throughput.

[00:00] Samir Patel: hey everyone, thanks for jumping on, quick roll call?
[00:08] Michael Torres: yeah, hi this is Michael, Priya and Daniel are here too
[00:11] Priya Rao: hi
[00:12] Daniel Kim: hi all
[00:15] Samir Patel: great, goal for today is to walk through what we've seen in the initial traces, compare TensorRT-LLM and vLLM runs, and agree on a benchmark plan. I'll hand over to Aisha for the profiling overview.
[00:30] Aisha Chen: thanks, so first slide, high-level: we profiled your RL inference loop, 8k context, batch size 1-4, tail latency spikes around 300-500ms under bursty load. We pulled kernel timelines, cudagraph capture windows, and quantified KV cache misses which correlate with token re-generation on cold starts.
[00:55] Marco Diaz: one important piece is kernel selection - TRT-LLM tends to pick fused attention+kv kernels that reduce launch overhead, vLLM using Triton-backed kernels shows more fine-grained ops so slightly different latency characteristics. In our run TRT-LLM had better p50 and p90 but p99s were mixed depending on cudagraph warmup.
[01:20] Priya Rao: when you say cudagraph warmup can you elaborate, we saw latency drop after a few requests but then sometimes a spike reappeared after a minute of inactivity
[01:28] Aisha Chen: yes, two effects: cudagraph capture is beneficial when the control flow is stable - same sequence length and prompt patterns. But if your workload has variable sequence lengths or branching (like RL sampling steps), captures can be re-taken and that causes brief jank while the graph is recreated. Also driver-level eviction can drop captured graphs under memory pressure.
[01:50] Daniel Kim: our infra runs multiple tenants, could that cause eviction? GPUs are 80GB A100s but we do run other jobs occasionally.
[01:57] Marco Diaz: absolutely, concurrent allocations plus host-side fragmentation can cause the driver to free cudagraphs. We noticed on testbed when we marked GPU as isolated (exclusive compute) the cudagraph persistence improved p99 by ~80ms.
[02:15] Michael Torres: ok that maps to our ops setup. On quantization, we tried 4-bit on some models and saw small quality drift but big throughput gains, curious how Redwood thinks about kernel selection for quantized paths.
[02:25] Aisha Chen: with quantization we surface different kernels - int8/int4 paths use rematerialized GEMMs or custom fused kernels. TensorRT-LLM precomputes some pathways and can avoid dynamic type conversions, vLLM has plugin-based int8 which depends on Triton ops maturity. The kernel selector in our runtime chooses based on model profile and measured latency/accuracy tradeoffs.
[02:50] Priya Rao: can you show the actual traces?
[02:52] Aisha Chen: yeah, demos coming up - sharing screen now
[03:05] [03:05] Aisha Chen: here's a captured timeline, x-axis is time, each strand is streaming CUDA kernel launches. You can see fused attention kernels at baseline, then at 00:23 a cudagraph re-capture event (you see a small gap where kernels fire, then a brief recompile).
[03:30] Marco Diaz: note the kernel concurrency too - when batching increases we do more concurrent kernel launches which amortizes overhead, but if batch size jumps then memcopies increase and that can push p99 up. For Helix's workload where you have many short requests, small batches with prefix caching looked best.
[03:58] Daniel Kim: prefix caching - is that the KV cache sizing conversation? We have limited GPU memory peaks around token 6k with some requests going to 8k.
[04:05] Aisha Chen: yes, KV cache sizing is critical. We recommend dynamic KV eviction thresholds: keep most recent N tokens per request in GPU memory and fall back to CPU cache after threshold. For your 80GB GPUs with other tenants, a conservative setting is 6k tokens on-GPU and rest in host-pinned memory. That reduced GPU OOMs in our tests.
[04:35] Priya Rao: how does that impact latency when it falls back to CPU?
[04:38] Marco Diaz: there is a penalty, roughly 20-60ms depending on host bus throughput. But you can hide some of it with async prefetching if your pattern is predictable.
[04:52] [04:52] Michael Torres: what's Redwood's approach to batching for RL workloads where sampling and small step sizes are common?
[04:58] Samir Patel: we recommend micro-batching + continuous batching where a short buffer stitches requests within a tight window (e.g., 5-10ms) to form small batches. You get throughput with bounded latency. We also have adaptive policies to drop into single-request mode when tail latency SLOs are nearing breach.
[05:20] Priya Rao: sounds good. Any comments on TensorRT vs vLLM inference accuracy drift with 4-bit quant? We saw some hallucination increase on certain prompts.
[05:28] Aisha Chen: quantization-aware calibration helps - TensorRT-LLM has per-channel scales which generally preserve sampling behavior better. For aggressive 4-bit schemes you should run localized evals on a held-out prompt set; Redwood's Optimize service can run regression tests and flag regressions.
[05:50] Marco Diaz: also consider hybrid quant: keep attention and layernorm in float16 and quantize large matmuls. That often gives 70-90% of throughput gains with much smaller accuracy impact.
[06:08] Daniel Kim: on the on-prem side, what about GPU driver versions and CUDA compatibility? We have mixed nodes (A100 and H100) and the drivers differ.
[06:20] Aisha Chen: mixed fleets complicate kernel selection. Our runtime compiles kernels per device capability and selects per-request. For H100 we use newer kernels (sm90) and they can be much faster for certain fused ops. We recommend a uniform driver baseline where possible; driver mismatches are a major source of nondeterministic performance.
[06:45] Priya Rao: any consideration for using TensorRT engine caching to avoid re-building engines during deploys?
[06:51] Marco Diaz: yes, we persist TensorRT engines to disk and snapshot them as part of model artifacts. That cuts cold-starts dramatically. But keep them tied to CUDA/driver versions and GPU arch, otherwise engines are invalid.
[07:10] [07:10] Michael Torres: can Redwood run a side-by-side benchmark with our RL payload? We want both p50/p90/p99 and cost per token numbers.
[07:15] Samir Patel: absolutely, that's the ask we'll run. We'll also include kernel-level traces and cudagraph timelines. We'll need a sample load script and some S3 access.
[07:28] Priya Rao: I'll send a synthetic workload that matches our 80% short-turn sampling and 20% long-generation cases.
[07:34] Daniel Kim: and we'll share infra topology and a list of noisy co-tenants that might run concurrently.
[07:40] Aisha Chen: great. Quick note on Triton vs vLLM naming - sometimes the transcript or tools mislabel Triton/Triton Inference Server as "Trident" or similar - ignore that in earlier notes, we used Triton/Triton-backed kernels in vLLM path.
[07:58] Marco Diaz: one more micro-optimization: try to pin CUDA streams per-request to reduce stream contention; that reduced observed jitter in our internal tests by ~30ms p99.
[08:12] Priya Rao: good to know.
[08:16] [08:16] Michael Torres: any security or VPC implications for running dedicated inference? we have strict egress controls and FIPS requirements for keys.
[08:25] Samir Patel: for on-prem/VPC we can support customer-managed KMS and private control plane. We'll provide docs (SOC2/ISO artifacts) and sample network diagrams. For FIPS, we may need specific lib builds; we will check compatibility with your compliance team.
[08:45] Sara Liu: for audit logs, can we get token-level tracing? we need to ensure PII is redacted server-side.
[08:52] Aisha Chen: Redwood supports token-level cost breakdowns and audit logs; for PII we can enable redaction in the ingestion pipeline or opt to route sensitive workloads to Private deployment with no logs retained. We'll follow up with security docs.
[09:12] [09:12] Michael Torres: ok let's recap next steps
[09:15] Samir Patel: recap: Redwood to run 48h benchmark with both TensorRT-LLM and vLLM configs; Helix to provide workload and infra details; Redwood to share engine configs and cudagraph/kernel traces; schedule follow-up week of 2026-11-16.
[09:35] Priya Rao: thanks everyone, I'll upload the workload to the shared bucket by Friday
[09:40] Daniel Kim: will do the infra topology doc as well
[09:42] Samir Patel: thanks all, we'll send a calendar invite for the follow-up and the S3 instructions now
[09:47] Michael Torres: thanks, bye
[09:48] End of recording
